correct_citation: Harris, R. A. (1999). The School Attendance Demonstration Project: Impact Analysis Using an Experimental and Longitudinal Research Design. ERIC ED441860.
design: Random assignment by DSS (2/3 treatment, 1/3 control); longitudinal follow-up Mar 1996-Mar 1998
population_location: AFDC-recipient students aged 16-18, San Diego County / San Diego Unified, California
outcome: 80% monthly attendance requirement met; dropout status (non-attendance in later month); graduation (June 1998 records)
effect_as_reported: Treatment more likely to meet 80% attendance rule (significant); no significant difference in mean dropout rates; logits show no group difference in graduation
excerpt: We found no evidence that graduation and dropout rates were affected by the program.
note: Attribution, design, place and null graduation/dropout finding confirmed. The treatment was an 80% attendance rule with AFDC benefit sanction plus orientation where non-compliers were screened for unmet social-service needs; the source does not describe it as case management. Graduation was partly a proxy measure.

correct_citation: Davis, J. M. V., & Heller, S. B. (2020). Rethinking the Benefits of Youth Employment Programs: The Heterogeneous Effects of Summer Jobs. Review of Economics and Statistics, 102(4), 664-677 (NBER WP 23443, 2017).
design: Two randomized field experiments (2012 and 2013 cohorts) of One Summer Plus supported summer jobs
population_location: Youth in Chicago (high-violence high schools; broader eligibility 2013)
outcome: Days present the year after; school persistence (graduated or still enrolled in CPS) from Chicago Public Schools records
effect_as_reported: No significant change in school persistence through start of third post-program year; CIs rule out more than 4-5 day increase in days present
excerpt: school persistence (either graduating from or continuing to attend the Chicago Public Schools) does not significantly change through the start of the third post-program school year.
note: Content verified from the NBER working-paper version; journal citation (vol 102, issue 4, pp. 664-677, 2020) confirmed via Crossref. Main effect is a large drop in violent-crime arrests.

correct_citation: Grossman, J. B., & Sipe, C. L. (1992). Summer Training and Education Program (STEP): Report on Long-Term Impacts. Philadelphia, PA: Public/Private Ventures. (WWC study 30518; WWC Intervention Report May 2009, ERIC ED505399)
design: Randomized controlled trial; STEP vs work-only (SYETP summer job) control; cohorts 2 and 3 meet WWC standards without reservations
population_location: Low-income 14-15-year-olds testing below grade level; five sites (Boston, Fresno, Portland, San Diego, Seattle)
outcome: Self-reported dropout and highest grade completed (follow-up interviews ~4 years after assignment)
effect_as_reported: Dropped out: cohort 2 29.2% vs 25.1%, cohort 3 21.6% vs 22.6%, not significant; highest grade 11.2 vs 11.2 and 10.8 vs 10.9; WWC rating no discernible effects (avg improvement index -2)
excerpt: The study found no statistically significant differences between STEP and control group youth in their self-reported dropout rates about four years after random assignment.
note: Only the WWC clearinghouse review (secondary) was fetched; the P/PV primary report could not be located online. The WWC study page's domain heading oddly says 'statistically significant negative effect' for staying in school, but individual findings are non-significant and the intervention report rates it 'no discernible effects'. The comparison was a summer job, not no treatment.

correct_citation: Bradshaw, C. P., Zmuda, J. H., Kellam, S. G., & Ialongo, N. S. (2009). Longitudinal Impact of Two Universal Preventive Interventions in First Grade on Educational Outcomes in High School. Journal of Educational Psychology, 101(4), 926-937. doi:10.1037/a0016586 (ERIC EJ860910; PMC3678772)
design: Randomized controlled trial; first-grade classrooms 1993-94 assigned to classroom-centered (Good Behavior Game + enhanced curriculum), Family-School Partnership, or control; followed to age 19
population_location: 678 urban, primarily African American children, Baltimore City
outcome: High school graduation or GED, from district data
effect_as_reported: CC: significant positive effect overall (B=0.532, OR=1.702, p<.05) and for girls (OR=2.118); adjusted graduation 61.9% CC vs 51.3% control; FSP: 57.3%, no significant effect on graduation
excerpt: With regard to high school graduation, there was a significant positive effect of the CC intervention in the overall sample ( B = 0.532, OR = 1.702, p < .05)
note: Graduation source is district records (plus GED). FSP had only one significant effect across outcomes, and it was not graduation.

correct_citation: Vitaro, F., Brendgen, M., & Tremblay, R. E. (1999). Prevention of School Dropout Through the Reduction of Disruptive Behaviors and School Failure in Elementary School. Journal of School Psychology, 37(2), 205-226. (ERIC EJ598786)
design: Preventive intervention evaluation (design details not in abstract)
population_location: Disruptive boys from low socioeconomic status
outcome: Later school dropout problems
effect_as_reported: Indirect effect on dropout via reduced grade retention/special-class placement; no direct effect reported in abstract; no size available
excerpt: Results show that the program had an indirect effect on later school dropout problems through its impact on grade retention/special education placement.
note: The cited title is truncated (real title adds 'and School Failure in Elementary School'). Only the ERIC abstract and Crossref metadata could be fetched; ScienceDirect blocked. Randomization, kindergarten timing, Montreal, the social-skills plus parent-training components and effect size could not be confirmed. The effect was indirect only.

correct_citation: Gonzales, N. A., Wong, J. J., Toomey, R. B., Millsap, R., Dumka, L. E., & Mauricio, A. M. (2014). School Engagement Mediates Long-Term Prevention Effects for Mexican American Adolescents. Prevention Science, 15(6), 929-939. doi:10.1007/s11121-013-0454-y (WWC study 85480; PMC4087099)
design: 5-year follow-up of a randomized trial; path models with 9th-grade school engagement as mediator; WWC: RCT, meets standards without reservations
population_location: 516 Mexican American 7th graders, four urban Title I schools, Southwestern metropolitan area (Bridges/Puentes)
outcome: Dropout at 12th-grade assessment, from youth report, parent report and school archival records (59% of sample)
effect_as_reported: Paper: significant indirect effect on dropout via engagement (ab = -0.062, CI -0.517 to -0.001). WWC: did not drop out 88% vs 75%, significant, improvement index 21 (n=420)
excerpt: A significant indirect effect for the intervention on T3 dropout through school engagement was found (ab = −0.062, CI (−0.517, −0.001)).
note: The authors report the dropout effect as indirect (mediated by engagement), not as a direct program effect. Dropout was mostly self- or parent-reported, with archival records for 59%. The WWC study page gives improvement index 21 (88 vs 75%), but the 'g about 0.54' figure is not shown on the fetched page (index 21 is consistent with g of about 0.55).

correct_citation: Dee, T. S., & Penner, E. K. (2019). My Brother's Keeper? The Impact of Targeted Educational Supports. CEPA Working Paper No. 19-07, Stanford Center for Education Policy Analysis (ERIC ED600998).
design: Difference-in-differences (and DDD) using staggered scale-up of AAMA across OUSD high schools and grades; school-grade-year panel
population_location: Black male (and female) high school students, Oakland Unified School District, California
outcome: Event dropout counts at school-grade-year level from California Department of Education files
effect_as_reported: AAMA access reduced Black male dropouts by 43% (5.2 to 3.0 per cohort of 61.3), ~3.6 pp gain in one-year persistence, concentrated in 9th grade; Black female dropout counts reduced ~29%
excerpt: We find that AAMA availability led to a significant reduction in the number of Black males who dropped out as well as smaller reductions among Black females, particularly in 9th grade.
note: Design, direction and size confirmed. The dropout data come from California Department of Education public school-grade counts, not student-level district records. The 2021 journal version was not fetched or checked.

correct_citation: Zhu, P., Nash, P., Solís-Román, C., Commins, N., & Martinez, L. (2026). Does an Early Social-Emotional Learning Program Have Lasting Academic Effects through High School? High School Follow-Up Findings from a Randomized Trial of INSIGHTS. MDRC (ERIC ED681730).
design: Cluster (school-level) randomized trial of INSIGHTS (K-1 temperament-based SEL), 13-year follow-up with administrative records
population_location: 1,329 students in 22 New York City public elementary schools
outcome: On-time New York State diploma (and with one-year delay), from NYC Public Schools and National Student Clearinghouse records
effect_as_reported: Full sample: on-time diploma 37.4% vs 37.1% (impact 0.4 pp, p=0.918); with delay 46.3% vs 48.7% (n.s.); low-income subgroup: no significant improvement in graduation
excerpt: The proportion of students who received a New York State diploma by the end of their expected senior year was also virtually identical—37.4 percent for INSIGHTS group students and 37.1 percent for attention-control group students.
note: College enrollment was about 6 pp lower for INSIGHTS (p=0.117). For the parent-consent subgroup, on-time diploma favored INSIGHTS by 9 pp (p=0.122, n.s.).

correct_citation: Bierman, K. L., Heinrichs, B. S., Welsh, J. A., Jones, D. E., & Crowley, D. M. (2025). How a Preschool Intervention Affected High School Outcomes: Longitudinal Pathways in a Randomized-Controlled Trial. Child Development. doi:10.1111/cdev.14235 (PMC12023813)
design: Randomized trial; Head Start classrooms randomized to REDI (N=192) or usual practice (N=164); followed to high school with mediation models
population_location: 356 children from 44 classrooms in 26 Head Start centers in three Pennsylvania counties
outcome: On-time graduation (school records and youth interviews), a secondary outcome
effect_as_reported: No direct impact on on-time graduation or GPA; indirect effects through earlier intervention gains
excerpt: REDI had no direct impact on GPA or on‐time graduation but promoted these outcomes indirectly mediated by earlier intervention effects.
note: All parts confirmed except location: the source says 'three Pennsylvania counties' (smaller urban, rural and small-town communities), not 'central Pennsylvania'. Graduation data covered 69% of the sample.

correct_citation: Pai, A. (2026). The Effect of School-Based Health Centers on Adolescent Mental Health and Behavior. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1452, Annenberg Institute at Brown University (ERIC ED681900).
design: Staggered difference-in-differences using timing of SBHC openings, with propensity-score matched control schools
population_location: K-12 schools in California
outcome: Suspension rates and dropout rates
effect_as_reported: Suspensions fell ~1.1 pp (18% vs matched schools); no effect on dropout rates
excerpt: There is no effect on dropout rates, indicating that the decline in suspensions is unlikely to be caused by crowd-out of delinquent behavior by an increase in dropping out.
note: Verified from the ERIC record abstract.

correct_citation: Truwit, M. (2025). Investigating the Promise of Integrated Student Supports: An Evaluation of the Community School Model in Tennessee. Peabody Journal of Education, 100(2), 252-282. doi:10.1080/0161956X.2025.2483144 (ERIC EJ1509139; ED681409)
design: Difference-in-differences with event-study specification using within-school transitions in community school status
population_location: Schools in Tennessee urban districts (statewide evaluation)
outcome: School dropout rate (also grade progression, chronic absenteeism, suspensions, test scores)
effect_as_reported: No change in dropout rate or grade progression; small ELA gains, lower suspension and mobility; increase in chronic absenteeism
excerpt: however, I find no change in math performance, grade progression, or dropout rate and a surprising increase in chronic absenteeism.
note: The surprising increase in chronic absenteeism matters for SPOTlight attendance use.

correct_citation: What Works Clearinghouse (2009, January). Wyman Teen Outreach Program (TOP). WWC Intervention Report, Dropout Prevention (ERIC ED503803).
design: WWC systematic review under Dropout Prevention protocol
population_location: Nine TOP studies (1988-2008); program for 12-17-year-olds
outcome: Effectiveness for dropout prevention
effect_as_reported: Seven in-scope studies did not meet evidence standards; two out of scope; no conclusions possible
excerpt: The lack of studies meeting WWC evidence standards means that, at this time, the WWC is unable to draw any conclusions based on research about the effectiveness or ineffectiveness of TOP.
note: The claim is about the clearinghouse's own rating, so the WWC report is the primary source here. Reasons: four studies used outcomes not defined for dropouts; three lacked baseline equivalence.

correct_citation: Heppen, J. B., Sorensen, N., Allensworth, E., Walters, K., Rickles, J., Taylor, S. S., & Michelman, V. (2017). design: Randomized controlled trial; students assigned to online or face-to-face summer algebra credit recovery
population_location: 1,224 ninth graders who failed algebra, 17 Chicago public high schools
outcome: Credit recovery, algebra posttest; second-year outcomes (math tests, subsequent math course passing, credits, on-track)
effect_as_reported: Credit recovery 66% online vs 78% f2f (d = -0.35); online lower posttest; no significant differences on second-year outcomes incl. on-track
excerpt: there was a 12-percentage-point difference in credit recovery rates by condition: 66% of students in the online course in contrast to 78% of students in the f2f course successfully recovered credit

(2018), as cited in ED659373, not from this paper or Allensworth et al. 2014. The given Semantic Scholar URL was not used; ERIC full text was.

correct_citation: Rickles, J., Peko-Spicer, S., Brodziak De Los Reyes, I., & Clements, P. (2023). Effects of Online Credit Recovery on High School Credit Accumulation and Graduation: Evidence from a Multisite Randomized Study. SREE 2023 conference abstract (ERIC ED659373). Journal: Peko-Spicer, S., Rickles, J., Clements, M., Lachowicz, M., & Brodziak de los Reyes, I. (2026). Does an Online Learning Approach to High School Credit Recovery Affect High School Graduation Rates? Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis (EJ1505887).
design: Multisite randomized study; random assignment within school-course-cohort blocks to online or teacher-directed (BAU) summer credit recovery
population_location: 613 Algebra 1 students (13 high schools) and 1,124 English 9 students (19 high schools), large urban district, 2017-18 and 2018-19 cohorts
outcome: Credit accumulation over four years; on-time high school graduation
effect_as_reported: SREE abstract: no findings yet. EEPA abstract: no statistically significant effect on graduation or credit accumulation; imprecise, differences not ruled out

correct_citation: Smerillo, N. E., Reynolds, A. J., Temple, J. A., & Ou, S.-R. (2018). Chronic Absence, Eighth-Grade Achievement, and High School Attainment in the Chicago Longitudinal Study. Journal of School Psychology, 67, 163-178. doi:10.1016/j.jsp.2017.11.001 (PMC6047866)
design: Longitudinal cohort; OLS, probit and IPWRA with covariates mostly measured in or before grade 4, including kindergarten cognitive composite and third-grade achievement
population_location: 1,148 participants in the Chicago Longitudinal Study (low-income, mostly Black, Chicago)
outcome: Chronic absence in grades 4-6 vs four-year graduation by diploma, diploma by age 21, any completion by age 21 (and 8th-grade achievement)
effect_as_reported: Chronic absence reduced probability of 4-year graduation by 18 pp, diploma by 21 by 17 pp, any completion by 21 by 11 pp; d = -0.17 for 8th-grade math
excerpt: chronic absence in the early middle grades was negatively associated (d=-0.17) with eighth-grade math achievement and reduced the probability of four-year graduation by diploma by 18 percentage points
note: Earlier achievement is controlled (kindergarten cognitive composite and third-grade achievement). The exposure is grades 4-6 only; no grades 7-8 chronic-absence exposure was found in the paper. The design is observational and associational.

correct_citation: Schoeneberger, J. A. (2012). Longitudinal Attendance Patterns: Developing High School Dropouts. The Clearing House, 85(1), 7-14. doi:10.1080/00098655.2011.603766 (ERIC EJ951297)
design: Group-based trajectory modeling of longitudinal attendance patterns
population_location: Students in one district (elementary and middle grades), per abstract
outcome: Attendance-trajectory group membership and dropout rates
effect_as_reported: Abstract says relation to dropout 'is revealed' but gives no direction or size
excerpt: Finally, the relation to attendance patterns and dropout rates is revealed.
note: Existence, author, year and design confirmed from the ERIC abstract only; the full text is closed (Taylor & Francis). The direction (chronic-absence trajectories have higher dropout), the size and the controls could not be verified.

correct_citation: Zheng, Y., Gao, X., Shen, J., Johnson, M. R., & Krenn, H. Y. (2023). A Meta-Analysis of the Predictors of On-Time High School Graduation in the United States. NASSP Bulletin, 107(2), 130-155. doi:10.1177/01926365231170404 (ERIC EJ1382176)
design: Meta-analysis of 47 articles (1985 to April 2022), four dimensions: student background, family support, school program and support, school climate
population_location: U.S. studies
outcome: On-time high school graduation
effect_as_reported: Twelve factors had statistically significant positive or negative effects; pooled sizes not available
excerpt: The current meta-analysis reviewed 47 articles published from 1985 to April 2022 and aggregated the effect in four dimensions: student background, family support, school program and support, and school climate
note: Only the abstract was reachable (the SAGE PDF is blocked by Cloudflare). Which predictors were significant and the pooled sizes for GPA, course failure, credits and attendance could not be verified. Fifth author: Krenn, H. Y.

correct_citation: Marlow, S. A., & Rehman, N. (2021). The relationship between family processes and school absenteeism and dropout: a meta-analysis. The Educational and Developmental Psychologist, 38(1), 3-23. doi:10.1080/20590776.2020.1834842
design: Meta-analysis of 33 studies
population_location: Primary and secondary school students
outcome: School absenteeism and dropout (combined and multiple-outcome analyses)
effect_as_reported: Significant negative relationship of positive family processes with absenteeism/dropout (strongest in primary school); NFP positively related (strongest in secondary); pooled r not in abstract
excerpt: The findings indicated a significant negative relationship between PFP and school absenteeism and dropout and a significant positive relationship between school absenteeism and dropout and NFP.
note: Only the abstract and metadata were reachable (full text closed). The pooled size for dropout specifically, and whether included estimates adjust for prior achievement, could not be verified. The abstract pools absenteeism and dropout.

correct_citation: McNeal, R. B., Jr. (1999). Parental Involvement as Social Capital: Differential Effectiveness on Science Achievement, Truancy, and Dropping Out. Social Forces, 78(1), 117-144. (ERIC EJ593784)
design: Analysis of NELS:88 data
population_location: U.S. national sample (NELS:88)
outcome: Science achievement, truancy, dropping out
effect_as_reported: Parental involvement generally explained behavioral (truancy, dropout) but not cognitive outcomes; greater effects for more affluent and white students
excerpt: Parental involvement generally explained behavioral but not cognitive outcomes and had greater effects for more affluent and white students.
note: Only the ERIC abstract was reachable (OUP/JSTOR are behind Cloudflare). The dimensions measured are listed (discussion, PTO involvement, monitoring, educational support), but which ones were significant for dropout, and whether prior achievement was controlled, could not be verified.

correct_citation: Oreopoulos, P., Brown, R. S., & Lavecchia, A. M. (2017). Pathways to Education: An Integrated Approach to Helping At-Risk High School Students. Journal of Political Economy, 125(4), 947-984 (NBER WP 20430, 2014).
design: Difference-in-differences comparing cohorts before and after program introduction in Regent Park (2001) and Rexdale/Lawrence Heights (2007) with other Toronto public housing projects
population_location: Students entering grade 9 from Toronto public housing projects
outcome: 5-year high school graduation (and postsecondary enrollment)
effect_as_reported: Regent Park 5-year graduation +15.2 pp (38.2% to 53.4%); Rexdale/LH +9.7 pp; about 40% relative increase
excerpt: the 2001 introduction of Pathways in Regent Park increased the 5 year graduation rate by 15.2 percentage points (from 38.2 percent to 53.4 percent)
note: Content verified from the NBER WP version; the journal citation is confirmed via Crossref. The paper reports results for the Toronto expansion sites Rexdale and Lawrence Heights. It lists the sites outside Toronto (Ottawa, Kitchener, Montreal and others) but does not report their effects.

correct_citation: Larson, K. A., & Rumberger, R. W. (1995). ALAS: Achievement for Latinos through Academic Success. In H. correct_citation: Mac Iver, M. A., Sheldon, S., Naeger, S., & Clark, E. (2017). Mentoring Students Back On-Track to Graduation: Program Results from Five Communities. Education and Urban Society, 49(7), 643-675. doi:10.1177/0013124516645164 (ERIC EJ1151186)

note: Verified from the ERIC abstract; volume, issue and pages not independently checked.
